# README.md

Source: https://github.com/tikhomirov/opencode-bootstrap/blob/main/README.md

<h1 align="center">🧠 OpenCode Bootstrap</h1>

<p align="center">Production-ready bootstrap for a stronger global OpenCode setup plus project-specific intelligence.</p>

<p align="center">
  <a href="./README.ru.md"><img src="https://img.shields.io/badge/README-Русский-1f6feb" alt="Russian README"></a>
  <img src="https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Linux%20%7C%20macOS%20%7C%20WSL-0ea5e9" alt="Platforms">
  <img src="https://img.shields.io/badge/windows-native%20unsupported-lightgrey" alt="Windows unsupported">
  <img src="https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green" alt="MIT License">
  <img src="https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/tikhomirov/opencode-bootstrap/ci.yml?branch=main&label=ci" alt="CI">
</p>

## What it gives you

- stronger global OpenCode defaults for daily work, planning, verification, debugging, and review;
- project bootstrap via `/ocb-project-init` that turns repo evidence + a short interview into project-specific rules;
- explicit project artifacts under `.opencode/project/` instead of “magic in chat history”;
- bounded workflow commands: explore, grounded analysis, plan, implement, verify, fix, evolve, and loop;
- a bundled `bundle-maintenance` skill for safely changing shipped artifacts, manifests, checksums, and smoke-test flows;
- GPT-first orchestration with explicit Anthropic routing for code generation and high-risk final review.

## Supported platforms

- Linux
- macOS
- WSL2

Not supported:

- native Windows

Clipboard helpers:

- Linux X11: `xclip`
- Linux Wayland: `wl-clipboard`
- macOS: `pngpaste` when Homebrew is available

## What gets installed

Global OpenCode bundle under `~/.config/opencode/`:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `opencode.json`
- `commands/*.md`
- `prompts/*.md`
- `agents/*.md`
- `skills/*/SKILL.md`
- `tools/*.ts`

Core agents include:

- primary: `fast`, `build`, `plan`, `deep`
- workflow: `project-bootstrapper`, `grounded-researcher`, `loop-orchestrator`, `project-evolver`
- support: `researcher`, `designer`, `planner`, `verifier`, `reviewer`, `docs-research`, `frontend-visual`, `implementer`, `final-reviewer`

Global commands include:

- `/ocb-start`
- `/ocb-project-init`
- `/ocb-explore`
- `/ocb-grounded`
- `/ocb-plan`
- `/ocb-implement`
- `/ocb-verify`
- `/ocb-fix`
- `/ocb-evolve`
- `/ocb-loop`

## Quick start

```bash
git clone git@github.com:tikhomirov/opencode-bootstrap.git
cd opencode-bootstrap
chmod +x bootstrap.sh scripts/verify.sh scripts/generate-checksums.sh
./bootstrap.sh
```

## If you are new, start here

After installation, remember one command:

```text
/ocb-start
```

What to do next:

1. Authenticate once with `opencode auth login`.
2. Open your repository with `cd /path/to/project && opencode`.
3. Type `/ocb-start`.
4. If the project is not yet initialized, it gives you one command to run. If it is already initialized, it shows a short numbered menu and then gives you one command to run.

The safe default path for most work is still:

```text
/ocb-project-init
/ocb-plan <task>
/ocb-implement
/ocb-verify
```

The bootstrap flow is:

1. preflight
2. install dependencies
3. install OpenCode if missing
4. deploy bundle to staging
5. verify staging
6. backup and promote

Useful flags:

```text
--dry-run
--verify-only
--skip-deps
--skip-opencode
--skip-backup
--target-dir PATH
--bundle-dir PATH
--opencode-version VERSION
```

## Secrets and auth

The bootstrap does **not** copy:

- `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`
- provider API keys
- MCP OAuth tokens
- shell profile secrets
- session history or cache files

Manual post-install steps:

```bash
opencode auth login
opencode auth list
opencode mcp list
```

## How project rules are applied

Project-specific rules are never applied globally and never written to an arbitrary repository silently.

The target project is the current OpenCode session root.

Recommended usage:

```bash
cd /path/to/project
opencode
```

Then inside OpenCode:

```text
/ocb-project-init
```

Flow:

1. OpenCode detects the current repository root
2. the command shows that path
3. it asks for explicit confirmation
4. only then does it write project-specific artifacts

If the detected path is wrong, stop and restart OpenCode from the correct repository root.

## What `/ocb-project-init` creates

Inside the current repository:

```text
.opencode/project/
```

Main artifacts:

- `PROJECT_PROFILE.json`
- `PROJECT_RULES.generated.md`
- `LEARNED_RULES.generated.md`
- `PLAN.md`
- `RESEARCH.md`
- `VERIFY.md`
- `patches/`
- `evolutions/`
- `loops/`

The local project `opencode.json` is updated so generated rule files are loaded through `instructions`.

## What to do after `/ocb-project-init`

Short version: after `/ocb-project-init`, use the `/ocb-*` commands for normal work. They tell OpenCode what you want to do and which project files to use.

If you are not sure what to type next, run `/ocb-start` and let it route you to the right workflow command.

The simplest beginner flow is:

1. Run `/ocb-project-init` once in the repository.
2. For a new task, run `/ocb-plan <what you want to change>`.
3. When the plan looks right, run `/ocb-implement`.
4. When the work is done, run `/ocb-verify`.

If you remember only one pattern, remember this:

```text
/ocb-project-init
/ocb-plan add X
/ocb-implement
/ocb-verify
```

If you remember only one command, remember this:

```text
/ocb-start
```

## Commands vs agents

If you are new to OpenCode, this part is important.

- The `/ocb-*` entries are ready-made commands. This is the main interface you should use in chat.
- `fast`, `build`, `plan`, and `deep` in the agent selector are base agents. Think of them as internal work modes.
- A command already picks the right mode and instructions for you. For example, `/ocb-plan` starts the planning flow, and `/ocb-implement` starts the implementation flow.
- In normal work, prefer `/ocb-*` commands. Switch base agents manually only if you already understand the difference.

Why this is useful:

- commands are easier for beginners because they say exactly what you want: explore, plan, implement, verify, fix
- commands reuse the project files created by `/ocb-project-init`
- commands keep work structured, so OpenCode is less likely to skip planning or verification
- commands write useful artifacts such as `PLAN.md`, `RESEARCH.md`, `VERIFY.md`, and patch history

## Which command should I use?

| Situation | Use this | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| You are not sure what to type next | `/ocb-start` | A simple next step for setup or the right workflow command |
| You want to build something new safely | `/ocb-plan <task>` | A step-by-step plan in `.opencode/project/PLAN.md` |
| The plan is ready and you want code changes | `/ocb-implement` | Code changes guided by the saved plan and project rules |
| You want to check whether the work is correct | `/ocb-verify` | A verification summary in `.opencode/project/VERIFY.md` |
| Something is broken | `/ocb-fix <bug>` | Debugging first, then a small fix and a patch note |
| You are not ready to choose a solution | `/ocb-explore <topic>` | Options, pros and cons, and research notes |
| You want a strict factual answer | `/ocb-grounded <question>` | An evidence-only answer with no guessing |
| The same mistakes keep happening | `/ocb-evolve` | Stronger learned project rules from past fixes |
| The task needs several controlled rounds | `/ocb-loop new <task>` | A bounded iterative workflow with saved state |

## Beginner examples

Unsure where to begin:

```text
/ocb-start
```

New feature:

```text
/ocb-project-init
/ocb-plan add a command to check bundle health
/ocb-implement
/ocb-verify
```

Bugfix:

```text
/ocb-project-init
/ocb-fix the README says to run a command that does not exist
/ocb-verify
```

Research before coding:

```text
/ocb-project-init
/ocb-explore what is the safest way to verify the bundle after install?
/ocb-plan improve bundle verification without breaking bootstrap
```

Need a strict factual answer:

```text
/ocb-grounded which files define the shipped OpenCode bundle?
```

## Daily workflow

- Main path for most work: `/ocb-plan -> /ocb-implement -> /ocb-verify`
- Use `/ocb-explore` before planning if you are still choosing between options
- Use `/ocb-grounded` when you need a strict evidence-only answer
- Use `/ocb-fix` instead of `/ocb-plan` when something is already broken and needs debugging first
- Use `/ocb-evolve` after several fixes to improve learned project rules
- Use `/ocb-loop` only for bigger tasks that may need several controlled rounds

## Verification

Run at any time:

```bash
./scripts/verify.sh
```

It checks:

- bundle file presence
- OpenCode availability
- required agents
- MCP configuration (`playwright`, `context7`)
- enabled provider routing for `openai` and `anthropic`
- `fast -> openai/gpt-5.4`
- `implementer -> Claude Sonnet`
- `final-reviewer -> Claude Opus`

## Routing policy

- `fast` and `build` use GPT-5.4 for orchestration, repo research, planning, and verification
- `implementer` uses Claude Sonnet for write-heavy code generation and substantial refactors
- `final-reviewer` uses Claude Opus only for large or risky final review passes
- if evidence is insufficient, agents should stop, name the missing evidence, and avoid guessing

## Repository layout

```text
.
├── bootstrap.sh
├── README.md
├── README.ru.md
├── PROJECT_INTELLIGENCE_PLAN.md
├── bundle/
│   ├── AGENTS.md
│   ├── MANIFEST.txt
│   ├── VERSION
│   ├── checksums.txt
│   ├── commands/
│   ├── opencode.json
│   ├── prompts/
│   ├── agents/
│   ├── skills/
│   └── tools/
└── scripts/
    ├── generate-checksums.sh
    └── verify.sh
```

## Operational assumptions

- one write-heavy agent per project at a time
- no `git worktree` dependency
- logs, tests, diagnostics, and browser evidence are primary debugging inputs
- global config stays generic; project specifics are generated per repository

## Maintenance

When updating the bundle:

1. update files under `bundle/`
2. update `bundle/VERSION`
3. run `./scripts/generate-checksums.sh`
4. run `./scripts/verify.sh --target-dir "$HOME/.config/opencode"` if needed
5. update `CHANGELOG.md`

## Evaluation

- use `EVALUATION.md` for a repeatable golden-task checklist and A/B comparison method between baseline OpenCode and the bundled setup

# AGENTS.md

Source: https://github.com/tikhomirov/opencode-bootstrap/blob/main/AGENTS.md

# AGENTS.md

## Purpose
- This repository ships an OpenCode bootstrap bundle, not a conventional app or library.
- The primary deliverable is `bootstrap.sh` plus the curated payload under `bundle/`.
- Optimize for reproducibility, auditability, and safe local installation on Linux, macOS, and WSL.
- Keep changes minimal, reviewable, and tightly scoped.

## Rule Sources
- Repo-specific instructions live in this file.
- Shipped global agent rules live in `bundle/AGENTS.md`.
- Shipped prompts, agents, and commands live in `bundle/prompts/*.md`, `bundle/agents/*.md`, and `bundle/commands/*.md`.
- No `.cursorrules`, `.cursor/rules/`, or `.github/copilot-instructions.md` files were found.

## Working Model
- Follow: Research -> Design -> Plan -> Implement -> Verify -> Review for non-trivial changes.
- For small fixes, compress the flow, but still verify before finishing.
- Read the affected scripts, bundle files, and CI workflow before editing, and prefer the smallest safe change.
- Treat `.opencode/project/` as local repo intelligence, not shipped bundle content.

## Repository Map
- `bootstrap.sh`: main installer, dependency bootstrap, verification entry point, and promotion flow.
- `scripts/verify.sh`: thin wrapper around `./bootstrap.sh --verify-only`.
- `scripts/generate-checksums.sh`: regenerates or checks `bundle/checksums.txt`.
- `bundle/`: shipped runtime payload including config, prompts, commands, agents, skills, and tools.
- `bundle/tools/*.ts`: custom tool implementations shipped inside the bundle.
- `bundle/opencode.json`: shipped runtime configuration and MCP wiring.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: source of truth for automated verification and platform coverage.

## Build, Lint, and Test Commands
- There is no normal application build step and no dedicated lint tool like ESLint, Ruff, or ShellCheck.
- Syntax validation is POSIX shell parsing via `sh -n`, and the main verification surface is checksum validation plus disposable bootstrap smoke tests.

## Core Commands
- Make scripts executable once in a fresh clone: `chmod +x bootstrap.sh scripts/verify.sh scripts/generate-checksums.sh`
- Show installer options: `./bootstrap.sh --help`
- Dry-run install: `./bootstrap.sh --dry-run --target-dir /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-dry-run`
- Disposable install: `./bootstrap.sh --target-dir /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-test --force --skip-backup`
- Verify-only run: `./bootstrap.sh --verify-only --target-dir /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-test`
- Verify wrapper: `./scripts/verify.sh --target-dir /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-test`
- Check bundle checksums: `./scripts/generate-checksums.sh --check`
- Regenerate bundle checksums: `./scripts/generate-checksums.sh`

## Syntax Checks
- `sh -n bootstrap.sh`
- `sh -n scripts/verify.sh`
- `sh -n scripts/generate-checksums.sh`

## CI-Equivalent Local Verification
```bash
sh -n bootstrap.sh
sh -n scripts/verify.sh
sh -n scripts/generate-checksums.sh
./scripts/generate-checksums.sh --check
./bootstrap.sh --dry-run --target-dir /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-dry-run
./bootstrap.sh --target-dir /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-test --force --skip-backup
./scripts/verify.sh --target-dir /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-test
TARGET="/tmp/opencode-bootstrap-test"
cd "$TARGET"
OPENCODE_CONFIG="$TARGET/opencode.json" OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR="$TARGET" opencode serve --port 4110 >/tmp/opencode-bootstrap-serve.log 2>&1 &
SERVER_PID=$!
sleep 5
curl --noproxy '*' -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:4110/experimental/tool/ids" | tee /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-tool-ids.json
kill "$SERVER_PID"
wait "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
grep -q 'project_intelligence_status' /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-tool-ids.json
grep -q 'project_intelligence_apply' /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-tool-ids.json
grep -q 'loop_state_start' /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-tool-ids.json
grep -q 'loop_state_status' /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-tool-ids.json
```

## Single-Test Guidance
- There is no unit-test framework, no `package.json`, no `*test*` or `*spec*` suite, and no true single-test command in this repo.
- The closest equivalent is to run the narrowest verification command that exercises the changed surface.
- For shell syntax only: `sh -n path/to/script.sh`
- For checksum logic only: `./scripts/generate-checksums.sh --check`
- For installer flow without writes: `./bootstrap.sh --dry-run --target-dir /tmp/<name>`
- For verification logic only: `./bootstrap.sh --verify-only --target-dir /tmp/<name>`
- For end-to-end bootstrap behavior: `./bootstrap.sh --target-dir /tmp/<name> --force --skip-backup`

## Verification by Change Type
- `bootstrap.sh` changed: run syntax checks, dry-run install, and disposable install.
- `scripts/verify.sh` changed: run syntax checks plus `./scripts/verify.sh --target-dir /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-test`.
- `scripts/generate-checksums.sh` changed: run syntax checks plus `./scripts/generate-checksums.sh --check`.
- Anything under `bundle/` changed: regenerate `bundle/checksums.txt`, run disposable install plus `./scripts/verify.sh`, and include the CI-equivalent custom tool smoke test when `bundle/tools/*.ts` or `bundle/opencode.json` changed.

## Change Expectations
- Treat `bundle/` as shipped artifact content.
- If the shipped file set changes, update `bundle/MANIFEST.txt`.
- If you modify anything under `bundle/`, regenerate `bundle/checksums.txt`.
- If shipped bundle behavior changes materially, review whether `bundle/VERSION` should be bumped.
- Preserve installer idempotence, path safety, and backup protections; test against disposable directories under `/tmp`.

## Formatting and File Conventions
- Follow `.editorconfig`: UTF-8, LF, final newline, spaces, and 2-space indentation for `*.sh`, `*.md`, and `*.txt`.
- Use ASCII by default.
- Match the surrounding file style instead of reformatting unrelated sections.

## Shell Style
- Write POSIX `sh`, not Bash-specific syntax, unless the file already requires something else.
- Start shell scripts with `#!/bin/sh` and `set -eu`.
- Quote variable expansions unless unquoted expansion is clearly intended.
- Prefer helper functions for repeated behavior, use `case` for branching, and `command -v` for capability checks.
- Keep globals in uppercase snake case.
- Keep function names in lowercase snake case.
- Follow the existing `log`, `warn`, and `die` pattern for user-facing messages.
- Fail fast with actionable errors instead of silently continuing.

## TypeScript Style in `bundle/tools/`
- Use ESM with top-level `import` statements.
- Prefer `node:` imports for Node built-ins.
- Match the existing no-semicolon style.
- Prefer `async`/`await` over raw promise chains and use small helpers to keep tool `execute` handlers focused.
- Write JSON files with `JSON.stringify(value, null, 2)` plus a trailing newline.
- Validate filesystem paths and user input before writing.

## Imports and Dependencies
- Keep imports grouped at the top of the file.
- Import only what the file uses.
- Prefer built-in Node modules and existing utilities before introducing new dependencies or abstractions.

## Types and Data Handling
- Prefer explicit TypeScript aliases for JSON-like data passed through tools.
- Narrow unknown input before using it, and validate that parsed JSON has the expected shape.
- Avoid changing serialized field names unless the task explicitly requires it.

## Naming Conventions
- Shell variables: uppercase snake case for globals, lowercase snake case for locals when practical.
- Shell functions: lowercase snake case.
- TypeScript functions and variables: camelCase.
- Type aliases and exported tool bindings: PascalCase for types, concise lower-case export names matching existing tool patterns.
- Filenames: keep existing naming conventions; do not rename shipped files without strong reason.

## Error Handling and Safety
- Throw explicit `Error` values with actionable messages in TypeScript.
- In shell, use `die` for hard failures and `warn` for non-fatal conditions.
- Do not swallow errors unless there is a clear fallback path.
- Validate target paths carefully; this repo intentionally blocks unsafe install destinations.
- Do not weaken verification, backup, or path-safety logic without strong justification.

## Editing Guidance
- Read `.github/workflows/ci.yml` before changing verification expectations.
- Keep diffs narrow and easy to audit.
- Preserve user changes outside the scoped fix.
- Avoid speculative refactors in shipped bundle files.
- If a required verification step cannot be run locally, say so explicitly.

## Practical Advice for Agents
- Start from the repo root so relative paths in scripts behave as expected.
- Prefer `--target-dir /tmp/<name>` for any install or verify smoke test.
- When in doubt, mirror CI behavior from `.github/workflows/ci.yml` rather than inventing a new workflow.

---

# Contributing

Source: https://github.com/tikhomirov/opencode-bootstrap/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md

# Contributing

Thanks for contributing to `opencode-bootstrap`.

## Scope

This repository is focused on one thing: reproducible bootstrap of a curated global OpenCode setup for Linux, macOS, and WSL.

Please keep changes aligned with that goal.

## Principles

- Prefer minimal and reviewable diffs.
- Keep the bootstrap flow idempotent.
- Do not add secrets, tokens, or machine-specific credentials.
- Keep MCP usage intentionally small.
- Preserve Linux + macOS + WSL compatibility.

## Before opening a PR

Run at least:

```bash
sh -n bootstrap.sh
sh -n scripts/verify.sh
sh -n scripts/generate-checksums.sh
./scripts/generate-checksums.sh --check
./bootstrap.sh --dry-run --target-dir /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-dry-run
./bootstrap.sh --target-dir /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-test --force --skip-backup
./scripts/verify.sh --target-dir /tmp/opencode-bootstrap-test
```

Then clean up temporary directories.

If you touch custom tools, also smoke-test tool loading through `opencode serve` and check that the expected tool IDs are present.

## Bundle changes

If you change anything under `bundle/`:

1. update the relevant files
2. regenerate `bundle/checksums.txt`
3. run the bootstrap smoke checks
4. update `CHANGELOG.md` if the change is user-visible

## Security

Do not commit:

- `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`
- API keys
- OAuth tokens
- session exports containing secrets
- machine-specific shell profile data

# OpenCode Evaluation Guide

Source: https://github.com/tikhomirov/opencode-bootstrap/blob/main/EVALUATION.md

# OpenCode Evaluation Guide

Use this guide to compare OpenCode behavior with the bootstrap bundle enabled versus a baseline setup.

## A/B setup

Run the same tasks against two installs:

- A: baseline OpenCode config without this bundle
- B: OpenCode config produced by this bundle

Keep these constant between runs:

- same repository snapshot
- same task wording
- same provider accounts and limits
- same MCP availability
- same verification commands

Recommended pattern:

1. Prepare a disposable target for the bundled setup.
2. Keep a copy of the baseline global config or use a second disposable target.
3. Execute the golden tasks below in both environments.
4. Record metrics in a sheet or dashboard.

## Golden tasks

Score each task on a 1-5 scale unless the metric is objective.

### 1. Evidence-only question

Prompt:

```text
Inspect this repository and answer only from verified evidence: what is the main shipped artifact, how is verification performed, and which files define global OpenCode behavior?
```

Measure:

- correctness
- unsupported claims count
- file-reference quality
- response latency

### 2. Planning task

Prompt:

```text
Create an implementation plan to tighten the default bash safety policy without breaking normal development workflows.
```

Measure:

- identifies likely files before proposing edits
- includes acceptance criteria
- includes verification steps
- lists risks and assumptions

### 3. Small bugfix

Prompt:

```text
Fix a small documentation inconsistency in this repository and verify the change.
```

Measure:

- scope control
- unnecessary file changes count
- verification completeness
- whether routing stays disciplined

### 4. Write-heavy implementation

Prompt:

```text
Add a new workflow command that documents a repository audit checklist and wire it consistently with the existing command set.
```

Measure:

- whether GPT orchestrates and `implementer` handles write-heavy work
- consistency with repo patterns
- completeness of verification
- diff quality

### 5. Verification task

Prompt:

```text
Verify whether the current bundle is internally consistent and summarize any gaps.
```

Measure:

- uses actual repo verification commands
- distinguishes passed checks from unverified areas
- avoids broad hand-waving

### 6. Review task

Prompt:

```text
Review the current working tree for routing and prompt quality regressions.
```

Measure:

- regression-finding quality
- signal-to-noise ratio
- whether findings match the actual diff

### 7. Ambiguous request handling

Prompt:

```text
Improve the quality of the agents in this repository.
```

Measure:

- whether the agent researches first
- whether it narrows scope from repository evidence
- whether it asks at most one necessary question when truly blocked

## Core metrics

Track these per run:

- task id
- environment: baseline or bundled
- model path chosen
- subagents used
- tools used
- total tokens
- input tokens
- output tokens
- wall-clock time
- command count
- verification commands run
- file count changed
- diff size
- user follow-up needed
- success or failure
- failure reason
- score: correctness
- score: predictability
- score: rule compliance
- score: efficiency

## Suggested scoring rubric

- `correctness`: did it solve the asked task?
- `predictability`: did it follow the expected workflow and routing?
- `rule_compliance`: did it obey repo rules, safety rules, and verification requirements?
- `efficiency`: did it avoid wasted turns, wasted tools, and irrelevant edits?

Use a weighted score if needed:

```text
overall = 0.40 * correctness
        + 0.25 * predictability
        + 0.20 * rule_compliance
        + 0.15 * efficiency
```

## Dashboard ideas

You can build a lightweight dashboard if you capture run events.

Recommended event model:

- run started
- model selected
- subagent invoked
- tool invoked
- tool completed
- verification started
- verification completed
- run finished

Useful dashboard slices:

- success rate by task type
- mean tokens by task type
- mean time by task type
- subagent usage frequency
- tool usage frequency
- verification rate
- average score by environment
- cost by environment
- failure reasons over time

## Practical collection options

### Option A: simple and fast

- store each run as one JSON row
- append to a local SQLite database or JSONL file
- visualize with Metabase, Grafana, or a small local web UI

### Option B: provider-aware analytics

- use an API gateway or proxy that logs provider requests
- record token usage, latency, errors, and model ids
- join provider metrics with task-level outcomes from your evaluation sheet

### Option C: full session telemetry

- instrument OpenCode runtime events or wrap `opencode run`
- record prompt, agent, subagent, tool calls, commands, and outcome
- emit structured events to Postgres, ClickHouse, or OpenTelemetry

## Minimum viable analytics stack

- collector: wrapper script around `opencode run`
- storage: SQLite or Postgres
- event format: JSONL
- dashboard: Metabase or Grafana

Minimum tables:

- `runs`
- `events`
- `tool_calls`
- `verifications`
- `scores`

## Important cautions

- do not store raw prompts or diffs if they may contain secrets
- hash repository names if needed
- separate provider metrics from sensitive task content
- keep baseline and bundled runs as comparable as possible

---

# Project Intelligence Plan

Source: https://github.com/tikhomirov/opencode-bootstrap/blob/main/PROJECT_INTELLIGENCE_PLAN.md

# Project Intelligence Plan

## Goal

Upgrade `opencode-bootstrap` from a global OpenCode baseline into a ready-to-use developer intelligence layer that:

- improves OpenCode globally without hardcoding language/framework stacks into the global layer;
- bootstraps project-specific intelligence through an interview-driven workflow;
- materializes the result into project artifacts instead of leaving it inside chat history;
- adds bounded loop workflows for complex iterative work;
- adds a learning loop so bug fixes gradually improve future agent behavior;
- keeps Linux, macOS, and WSL support;
- avoids `git worktree` dependency and assumes one write-heavy agent per project at a time.

## Architectural Decision

The system uses four layers.

### 1. Global baseline

Lives in the installed global OpenCode config and stays universal.

Contains:

- model routing
- global agents
- global commands
- global skills
- global MCP/tool policy
- global debugging discipline

Does not contain:

- framework-specific project rules
- language-specific project conventions
- project-local commands

### 2. Project bootstrap wizard

Entry point for project-level setup.

Responsibilities:

- inspect the current repository
- ask follow-up questions when repo evidence is insufficient
- capture stack, versions, tools, workflow, and verification preferences
- generate project overlay artifacts

### 3. Project overlay

Materialized project-specific intelligence, written into the current repository.

Primary artifacts:

```text
.opencode/project/
  PROJECT_PROFILE.json
  PROJECT_RULES.generated.md
  LEARNED_RULES.generated.md
  PLAN.md
  RESEARCH.md
  VERIFY.md
  patches/
  evolutions/
  loops/
```

Root-level integration:

- project-local `opencode.json` includes generated instructions from `.opencode/project/`
- no requirement to overwrite project `AGENTS.md`

### 4. Loop and learning system

Adds bounded iterative workflows and project learning artifacts.

Loop artifacts:

```text
.opencode/project/loops/current.json
.opencode/project/loops/<alias>/run.json
.opencode/project/loops/<alias>/history.jsonl
.opencode/project/loops/<alias>/artifact.md
```

Learning artifacts:

```text
.opencode/project/patches/*.md
.opencode/project/evolutions/*.md
```

## What We Borrow from AI Factory

### Adopt

- command-driven UX
- artifact-driven workflow
- project configuration as a first-class workflow
- explicit persisted plan/research/fix artifacts
- bounded loop with state on disk and resume support
- learning loop: fix -> patch -> evolve
- read-only verification gates

### Do not copy directly

- large preset catalogs as primary UX
- worktree-oriented parallel workflow
- marketplace/extensions as required first-version behavior
- a large number of commands without a tight orchestration model

## Final Product Shape

The final product should give the user:

- a stronger global OpenCode baseline;
- a project bootstrap command that understands the current repo and asks targeted questions;
- generated project rules that stay in the project and can be committed;
- explicit commands for explore, grounded analysis, planning, implementation, verification, fixing, evolving, and looping;
- learning from bug-fix history;
- a clear and safe target-project selection workflow.

## Commands to Add

Global commands to install with the bundle:

- `/ocb-project-init`
- `/ocb-explore`
- `/ocb-grounded`
- `/ocb-plan`
- `/ocb-implement`
- `/ocb-verify`
- `/ocb-fix`
- `/ocb-evolve`
- `/ocb-loop`

## Agents to Add

- `project-bootstrapper`
- `grounded-researcher`
- `loop-orchestrator`
- `project-evolver`

## Skills to Add

- `project-bootstrap-wizard`
- `grounded-analysis`
- `project-overlay-generation`
- `fix-patch-capture`
- `evolution-from-patches`
- `bounded-loop`

## Tools to Add

### `project_intelligence_*`

Purpose:

- detect project root and local overlay status
- apply `PROJECT_PROFILE.json`
- write generated rules
- update local `opencode.json` instructions safely
- persist workflow artifacts like `PLAN.md`, `RESEARCH.md`, `VERIFY.md`
- capture bug-fix patches
- update learned rules

### `loop_state_*`

Purpose:

- create loop run state
- read loop status
- update loop run state
- write artifact content
- append history events
- stop and clean loop runs safely

## Project Target Selection

Project-specific rules must never be applied silently to the wrong repo.

Selected design:

- target project is the current OpenCode session directory / repository root
- `/ocb-project-init` first detects the target root
- before writing anything, it explicitly asks the user to confirm the detected path
- if the path is wrong, the command aborts and the user reruns OpenCode from the correct project

Recommended usage:

```bash
cd /path/to/project
opencode
/ocb-project-init
```

Alternative:

```bash
opencode /path/to/project
/ocb-project-init
```

No cross-project writes are allowed by design.

## Questions the Wizard Must Ask

The wizard should infer what it can from the repository first, then ask only targeted follow-up questions.

Core dimensions:

- primary languages and versions
- backend framework and version
- frontend/UI stack
- testing stack
- CI system
- runtime and environment (Docker, local, WSL, etc.)
- package/build tools
- quality tools
- repo shape (single app, monorepo, plugin, package)
- verification strictness
- debugging preferences
- docs expectations
- security or destructive-action sensitivity

Answers may be free-form. The system should normalize them into a structured project profile.

## Files to Generate Per Project

### `PROJECT_PROFILE.json`

Machine-friendly source of truth for project specifics.

Contains:

- detected repo traits
- normalized stack information
- quality and workflow preferences
- canonical commands
- risk preferences

### `PROJECT_RULES.generated.md`

Human-readable project instructions used by OpenCode in that repo.

Contains:

- stack-specific constraints
- coding/testing/verification expectations
- canonical commands
- project debugging rules
- explicit compatibility expectations

### `LEARNED_RULES.generated.md`

Incrementally improved project-level guidance derived from patch history.

### `PLAN.md`, `RESEARCH.md`, `VERIFY.md`

Workflow artifacts created by project-specific commands.

## Loop Design

Loop is included in the first release, but stays bounded and explicit.

Supported flow:

1. `PLAN`
2. `PRODUCE`
3. `VERIFY`
4. `CRITIQUE`
5. `REFINE`

Properties:

- explicit max iterations
- explicit success criteria confirmation before start
- on-disk persistence
- compact iteration summaries
- stop reasons:
  - threshold reached
  - no major blockers
  - iteration limit
  - user stop
  - stagnation

## Learning Design

### `/ocb-fix`

Should:

- investigate bug using evidence
- fix or plan fix
- capture a patch artifact with:
  - problem
  - root cause
  - solution
  - prevention
  - tags

### `/ocb-evolve`

Should:

- read accumulated patches
- identify recurring prevention rules
- update `LEARNED_RULES.generated.md`
- write an evolution log into `.opencode/project/evolutions/`

## Implementation Scope

This is a single implementation milestone, but internally broken into batches for safe delivery.

### Batch 1 - Foundations

- add project intelligence plan document
- add new commands directory to bundle
- add new agents
- add new skills
- add new tools
- add manifest/checksum coverage

### Batch 2 - Project overlay engine

- implement project root detection
- implement project profile application
- implement generated rules writing
- implement local `opencode.json` instruction merge
- implement workflow artifact writing helpers

### Batch 3 - Wizard and project workflows

- implement `/ocb-project-init`
- implement `/ocb-explore`
- implement `/ocb-grounded`
- implement `/ocb-plan`
- implement `/ocb-implement`
- implement `/ocb-verify`

### Batch 4 - Fix/evolve/loop

- implement patch capture flow
- implement evolve flow and learned rules update
- implement bounded loop state and command workflow

### Batch 5 - Docs and verification

- document target-project selection clearly in both README files
- update repository layout docs
- update CI and bootstrap verification if needed
- regenerate checksums
- run local smoke tests

## Acceptance Criteria

The implementation is successful when:

- global bootstrap stays universal and does not become a stack-rule dump;
- `/ocb-project-init` can configure the current repo through an interview workflow;
- target project path is explicitly confirmed before project writes happen;
- project-specific intelligence is persisted under `.opencode/project/`;
- local `opencode.json` is updated to include generated project instructions safely;
- `/ocb-fix` creates patch artifacts;
- `/ocb-evolve` updates learned project rules from patch history;
- `/ocb-loop` can create, resume, inspect, and stop bounded loops;
- README explains exactly how the user chooses the project to configure;
- bootstrap verification and checksums remain green.

## Non-Goals for This Milestone

- native Windows support
- worktree-based parallel workflows
- marketplace/extension ecosystem
- giant preset catalogs of frameworks and stacks
- remote skill installation

## Expected User Experience

### Global setup

```bash
git clone <repo>
cd opencode-bootstrap
./bootstrap.sh
```

### Project setup

```bash
cd /path/to/project
opencode
/ocb-project-init
```

### Daily usage

```text
/ocb-explore ...
/ocb-grounded ...
/ocb-plan ...
/ocb-implement
/ocb-verify
/ocb-fix ...
/ocb-evolve
/ocb-loop new ...
```

# README.ru.md

Source: https://github.com/tikhomirov/opencode-bootstrap/blob/main/README.ru.md

<h1 align="center">🧠 OpenCode Bootstrap</h1>

<p align="center">Готовый bootstrap для усиления глобального OpenCode и генерации project-specific intelligence.</p>

<p align="center">
  <a href="./README.md"><img src="https://img.shields.io/badge/README-English-1f6feb" alt="English README"></a>
  <img src="https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Linux%20%7C%20macOS%20%7C%20WSL-0ea5e9" alt="Platforms">
  <img src="https://img.shields.io/badge/windows-native%20unsupported-lightgrey" alt="Windows unsupported">
  <img src="https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green" alt="MIT License">
  <img src="https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/tikhomirov/opencode-bootstrap/ci.yml?branch=main&label=ci" alt="CI">
</p>

## Что дает этот репозиторий

- усиленный глобальный baseline OpenCode для daily work, planning, verification, debugging и review;
- project bootstrap через `/ocb-project-init`, который превращает repo evidence + короткий диалог в проектные правила;
- явные project artifacts в `.opencode/project/`, а не “магию в истории чата”;
- bounded workflow-команды: explore, grounded analysis, plan, implement, verify, fix, evolve и loop;
- встроенный skill `bundle-maintenance` для безопасных изменений shipped artifacts, manifest/checksum файлов и smoke-test flow;
- GPT-first orchestration с явным Anthropic routing для code generation и high-risk final review.

## Поддерживаемые платформы

- Linux
- macOS
- WSL2

Не поддерживается:

- native Windows

Clipboard helpers:

- Linux X11: `xclip`
- Linux Wayland: `wl-clipboard`
- macOS: `pngpaste`, если доступен Homebrew

## Что устанавливается

Глобальный OpenCode bundle в `~/.config/opencode/`:

- `AGENTS.md`
- `opencode.json`
- `commands/*.md`
- `prompts/*.md`
- `agents/*.md`
- `skills/*/SKILL.md`
- `tools/*.ts`

Основные агенты:

- primary: `fast`, `build`, `plan`, `deep`
- workflow: `project-bootstrapper`, `grounded-researcher`, `loop-orchestrator`, `project-evolver`
- support: `researcher`, `designer`, `planner`, `verifier`, `reviewer`, `docs-research`, `frontend-visual`, `implementer`, `final-reviewer`

Глобальные команды:

- `/ocb-start`
- `/ocb-project-init`
- `/ocb-explore`
- `/ocb-grounded`
- `/ocb-plan`
- `/ocb-implement`
- `/ocb-verify`
- `/ocb-fix`
- `/ocb-evolve`
- `/ocb-loop`

## Быстрый старт

```bash
git clone git@github.com:tikhomirov/opencode-bootstrap.git
cd opencode-bootstrap
chmod +x bootstrap.sh scripts/verify.sh scripts/generate-checksums.sh
./bootstrap.sh
```

## Если вы новичок, начните отсюда

После установки запомните одну команду:

```text
/ocb-start
```

Что делать дальше:

1. Один раз выполните `opencode auth login`.
2. Откройте свой репозиторий через `cd /path/to/project && opencode`.
3. Введите `/ocb-start`.
4. Если проект ещё не инициализирован, команда сразу подскажет одно действие. Если уже инициализирован, покажет короткое нумерованное меню и затем даст одну команду для выполнения.

Безопасный путь по умолчанию для большинства задач остается таким:

```text
/ocb-project-init
/ocb-plan <задача>
/ocb-implement
/ocb-verify
```

Flow bootstrap:

1. preflight
2. install dependencies
3. install OpenCode if missing
4. deploy bundle to staging
5. verify staging
6. backup and promote

Полезные флаги:

```text
--dry-run
--verify-only
--skip-deps
--skip-opencode
--skip-backup
--target-dir PATH
--bundle-dir PATH
--opencode-version VERSION
```

## Секреты и auth

Bootstrap **не копирует**:

- `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`
- provider API keys
- MCP OAuth tokens
- секреты из shell profile
- историю сессий и cache files

Ручные шаги после установки:

```bash
opencode auth login
opencode auth list
opencode mcp list
```

## Как применяются проектные правила

Project-specific rules не применяются глобально и не записываются молча в случайный репозиторий.

Target project = текущий root OpenCode-сессии.

Рекомендуемый сценарий:

```bash
cd /path/to/project
opencode
```

Дальше внутри OpenCode:

```text
/ocb-project-init
```

Flow:

1. OpenCode определяет текущий корень репозитория
2. команда показывает этот путь
3. запрашивает явное подтверждение
4. только после подтверждения пишет project artifacts

Если путь определен неверно, нужно остановиться и перезапустить OpenCode из правильного корня проекта.

## Что создает `/ocb-project-init`

Внутри текущего репозитория:

```text
.opencode/project/
```

Основные артефакты:

- `PROJECT_PROFILE.json`
- `PROJECT_RULES.generated.md`
- `LEARNED_RULES.generated.md`
- `PLAN.md`
- `RESEARCH.md`
- `VERIFY.md`
- `patches/`
- `evolutions/`
- `loops/`

Локальный `opencode.json` проекта обновляется так, чтобы generated rule files подхватывались через `instructions`.

## Что делать после `/ocb-project-init`

Коротко: после `/ocb-project-init` для обычной работы используйте команды `/ocb-*`. Они подсказывают OpenCode, что именно вы хотите сделать и какие project files использовать.

Если не уверены, что вводить дальше, запустите `/ocb-start` и он направит вас к нужной workflow-команде.

Самый простой flow для новичка:

1. Один раз запускаете `/ocb-project-init` в репозитории.
2. Для новой задачи запускаете `/ocb-plan <что нужно изменить>`.
3. Когда план вас устраивает, запускаете `/ocb-implement`.
4. Когда работа закончена, запускаете `/ocb-verify`.

Если запомнить только один шаблон, пусть будет этот:

```text
/ocb-project-init
/ocb-plan add X
/ocb-implement
/ocb-verify
```

Если запомнить только одну команду, пусть будет эта:

```text
/ocb-start
```

## Команды и агенты - в чем разница

Если вы только начинаете пользоваться OpenCode, это важный момент.

- `/ocb-*` - это готовые команды. Именно ими лучше пользоваться в чате.
- `fast`, `build`, `plan` и `deep` в переключателе агента - это базовые агенты. Проще всего считать их внутренними режимами работы.
- Команда сама выбирает правильный режим и нужные инструкции. Например, `/ocb-plan` запускает режим планирования, а `/ocb-implement` - режим реализации.
- В обычной работе используйте `/ocb-*` команды. Базовых агентов вручную переключайте только если уже понимаете разницу.

Почему это полезно:

- команды проще для новичков, потому что прямо говорят, что вы хотите: исследовать, спланировать, реализовать, проверить, починить
- команды используют project files, созданные через `/ocb-project-init`
- команды держат работу структурированной, поэтому OpenCode реже пропускает планирование или проверку
- команды сохраняют полезные артефакты: `PLAN.md`, `RESEARCH.md`, `VERIFY.md` и историю фиксов

## Какую команду использовать?

| Ситуация | Что запускать | Что получите |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Не понимаете, что вводить дальше | `/ocb-start` | Простой следующий шаг: настройка проекта или нужная workflow-команда |
| Нужно безопасно сделать новую задачу | `/ocb-plan <задача>` | Пошаговый план в `.opencode/project/PLAN.md` |
| План уже готов и нужны изменения в коде | `/ocb-implement` | Изменения в коде по сохраненному плану и project rules |
| Нужно проверить, что все сделано правильно | `/ocb-verify` | Краткий отчет проверки в `.opencode/project/VERIFY.md` |
| Что-то сломалось | `/ocb-fix <баг>` | Сначала отладку, потом небольшой фикс и заметку о нем |
| Вы еще не выбрали решение | `/ocb-explore <тема>` | Варианты, плюсы и минусы, заметки исследования |
| Нужен строгий фактический ответ | `/ocb-grounded <вопрос>` | Ответ только на основе проверенных данных |
| Ошибки повторяются снова и снова | `/ocb-evolve` | Более сильные learned project rules из истории фиксов |
| Задача требует нескольких контролируемых итераций | `/ocb-loop new <задача>` | Bounded iterative workflow с сохраненным состоянием |

## Примеры для новичков

Не знаете, с чего начать:

```text
/ocb-start
```

Новая фича:

```text
/ocb-project-init
/ocb-plan добавить команду для проверки bundle
/ocb-implement
/ocb-verify
```

Багфикс:

```text
/ocb-project-init
/ocb-fix в README указана команда, которой не существует
/ocb-verify
```

Сначала исследовать, потом кодить:

```text
/ocb-project-init
/ocb-explore как безопаснее всего проверять bundle после установки?
/ocb-plan улучшить проверку bundle, не ломая bootstrap
```

Нужен строгий фактический ответ:

```text
/ocb-grounded какие файлы определяют shipped bundle OpenCode?
```

## Daily workflow

- Основной путь для большинства задач: `/ocb-plan -> /ocb-implement -> /ocb-verify`
- Используйте `/ocb-explore` перед планированием, если еще выбираете между вариантами
- Используйте `/ocb-grounded`, когда нужен строгий ответ только на основе подтвержденных данных
- Используйте `/ocb-fix` вместо `/ocb-plan`, если что-то уже сломано и сначала нужна отладка
- Используйте `/ocb-evolve` после нескольких фиксов, чтобы усилить learned project rules
- Используйте `/ocb-loop` только для более крупных задач, где может понадобиться несколько контролируемых раундов

## Проверка

Запуск:

```bash
./scripts/verify.sh
```

Проверяется:

- наличие bundle-файлов
- доступность OpenCode
- обязательные агенты
- MCP-конфигурация (`playwright`, `context7`)
- routing провайдеров для `openai` и `anthropic`
- `fast -> openai/gpt-5.4`
- `implementer -> Claude Sonnet`
- `final-reviewer -> Claude Opus`

## Политика routing

- `fast` и `build` используют GPT-5.4 для orchestration, исследования репозитория, планирования и верификации
- `implementer` использует Claude Sonnet для code generation и крупных refactor-шагов
- `final-reviewer` использует Claude Opus только для больших или рискованных финальных review
- если данных недостаточно, агент должен остановиться, назвать недостающие подтверждения и не гадать

## Структура репозитория

```text
.
├── bootstrap.sh
├── README.md
├── README.ru.md
├── PROJECT_INTELLIGENCE_PLAN.md
├── bundle/
│   ├── AGENTS.md
│   ├── MANIFEST.txt
│   ├── VERSION
│   ├── checksums.txt
│   ├── commands/
│   ├── opencode.json
│   ├── prompts/
│   ├── agents/
│   ├── skills/
│   └── tools/
└── scripts/
    ├── generate-checksums.sh
    └── verify.sh
```

## Operational assumptions

- один write-heavy агент на проект одновременно
- нет зависимости от `git worktree`
- логи, тесты, diagnostics и browser evidence — главные источники истины при отладке
- глобальный слой остается универсальным, а проектная специфика генерируется отдельно для каждого репозитория

## Поддержка bundle

При обновлении bundle:

1. обнови файлы в `bundle/`
2. обнови `bundle/VERSION`
3. запусти `./scripts/generate-checksums.sh`
4. при необходимости прогоняй `./scripts/verify.sh --target-dir "$HOME/.config/opencode"`
5. обнови `CHANGELOG.md`

## Evaluation

- используйте `EVALUATION.md` как repeatable golden-task checklist и способ A/B-сравнения baseline OpenCode с конфигурацией из bundle

# Security Policy

Source: https://github.com/tikhomirov/opencode-bootstrap/blob/main/SECURITY.md

# Security Policy

## Supported scope

This repository ships a bootstrap kit and a configuration bundle for OpenCode.

Security-sensitive areas include:

- shell command execution in `bootstrap.sh`
- file replacement and backup logic
- bundle integrity verification
- accidental inclusion of secrets in `bundle/`
- overly broad default permissions in `bundle/opencode.json`

## Reporting a vulnerability

If you discover a security issue, please do not open a public issue with exploit details.

Report it privately to the maintainer first and include:

- affected file(s)
- reproduction steps
- impact
- suggested fix, if available

## Security model notes

- This project does not ship provider credentials or auth tokens.
- Authentication remains a manual post-install step.
- The default bundle allows broad `bash` execution because OpenCode is intended to be an active coding agent.
- Review `bundle/opencode.json` before using this setup in sensitive environments.

---
